failure_modes: API client cannot connect if both TWS and Gateway are down

validation: Attempt API connection without TWS/Gateway running; confirm connection fails

title: API Order IDs must be strictly increasing

mechanism: API client maintains order ID counter; IB Gateway/TWS uses order ID to distinguish new vs. modified orders.
assumptions: Order ID counter persists across API sessions (needs verification for modern IB API)
No order ID wraparound or reset mechanism documented
failure_modes: Attempting to place new order with ID <= last used ID may fail silently or modify existing order
Order ID counter exhaustion (if 32-bit signed int used, max ~2B orders)
validation: Send two new orders with decreasing IDs; verify second order fails or modifies first order

Intraday initial margin changes may not be reflected immediately

title: Buying Power for margin accounts is 4x Available Funds

title: Regime change as collective trader behavior shift
claim: Regime change is a significant change in collective trading behavior in financial markets, reflected in observable price dynamics and their statistical properties.

Statistical properties of price movements can be used as proxies for regime identity

title: Directional Change as event-driven alternative to fixed-interval time series
claim: Directional Change (DC) is a data-driven approach that samples prices at event-driven thresholds (price movements exceeding a threshold) rather than fixed time intervals, allowing tick-by-tick monitoring.
support: Formalized in Appendix A; contrasted with time series sampling; shown to extract information not visible in fixed-interval analysis.
mechanism: When price change magnitude exceeds threshold θ, a directional change event is recorded; events define intrinsic-time sampling points rather than wall-clock time.
assumptions: Threshold θ is stable or knowable a priori
DC events are meaningful economic markers (not noise)
Intrinsic-time scale is relevant to trading decisions
failure_modes: Threshold selection arbitrary and sensitive to market conditions
Very low thresholds may capture noise; high thresholds miss slow regime shifts
Does not adapt to regime-dependent volatility

title: DC indicator R combines price movement and time duration
claim: The Directional Change indicator R measures return for each price trend, combining Total Price Movement (TMV) and Time to completion (T); both are orthogonal measures of volatility under DC.
support: Indicator R chosen by trial-and-error during methodology development; used as input to HMM for regime detection.
mechanism: R = f(TMV, T) where TMV is total magnitude and T is duration; log-transformed as LR[t] = log(R[t]) for HMM input.
assumptions: R is stationary or sufficiently stable for HMM fitting
Log transformation normalizes R distribution adequately
Combination of magnitude and duration is appropriate for regime identification
failure_modes: Trial-and-error selection not validated across other datasets
No sensitivity analysis on R functional form
Unknown how R behaves in regime-dependent volatility environments
validation: R tested on EUR-GBP, GBP-USD, EUR-USD 2016 data; successfully detects regime transitions missed by time-series volatility.

title: Realised volatility for time-series regime detection
claim: Realised Volatility (RV) computed from intra-day squared returns (e.g., 5-minute returns) serves as a time-series baseline for regime detection: RV(t) = sqrt(sum of squared intra-day returns).
support: Standard time-series volatility measure; used as comparison baseline to DC indicator in empirical study.
mechanism: Daily RV calculated as sqrt(sum of 5-minute squared log returns); fed into HMM alongside DC indicator for comparative regime detection.
assumptions: Daily aggregation is appropriate time scale
Gaussian distribution assumption in HMM fits RV values
failure_modes: Daily aggregation loses intra-day regime transitions
RV may be biased by market microstructure noise
validation: Comparison study: RV regimes aligned with Brexit 2016 volatility spike but missed some transitions detected by DC.

title: Two-state HMM for regime inference from indicators
claim: A two-state Hidden Markov Model with Gaussian observation density is used to infer hidden regime states from DC indicator R or time-series volatility; HMM parameter fitting via EM algorithm using depmixS4 R package.
support: Method implemented on second-by-second FX data May-July 2016; regimes detected successfully during Brexit period.
mechanism: HMM assumes two hidden regimes (Regime 1, Regime 2) generate observations; Viterbi or posterior inference assigns state to each observation; transitions between states mark regime changes.
assumptions: Two regimes are sufficient for the observation period
Gaussian emission distribution fits indicator values
Markovian assumption (future depends only on current state) holds
EM convergence guarantees global optimum (not always true)
failure_modes: Two-state model may miss additional regimes
Model fitting may converge to local optima
Gaussian assumption may not hold for heavy-tailed distributions
No automatic selection of number of states; requires domain knowledge
validation: Successfully applied to EUR-GBP, GBP-USD, EUR-USD; detected 2016 Brexit-related regime changes; regimes align with market events.

title: Brexit 2016: DC and time-series regime detection comparison on FX data
claim: During the 2016 Brexit period (May-July 2016), DC-based regime detection identified the same major regime changes as time-series volatility but also detected additional regime transitions not visible in daily realized volatility; DC approach is at least as effective and often complementary.
support: Second-by-second data for EUR-GBP, GBP-USD, EUR-USD from CCFEA/Kibot; both approaches detected volatility spike on June 24, 2016 (referendum result); DC detected additional finer-grained transitions.
mechanism: UK referendum June 23 resulted in unexpected exit vote; GBP plunged 30-year low; global stock sell-offs triggered. Both DC and RV indicators spiked during this period, indicating Regime 2 (higher volatility).
assumptions: Regime change definition (statistical shift) captures economically significant events
Threshold θ=0.4% appropriate for FX markets
failure_modes: Regimes may not be economically interpretable
Regime timing and boundaries depend on indicator and model choices
No causal link between identified regimes and trading performance established
validation: Study period well-documented historical event; regimes align with market news; replicable with public FX data and standard HMM tools.

title: Normal vs. Abnormal regime classification potential
claim: Regimes detected via DC+HMM can be classified into Normal (lower volatility, stable pricing) and Abnormal (crisis, high volatility) categories; this classification may identify early warning signals for market stress.
support: Authors characterize market regimes on 10 different markets; show statistical separation in indicator space between low- and high-volatility regimes.
mechanism: Regime 1 exhibits lower DC return R and lower realized volatility; Regime 2 exhibits higher values. Indicator-space clustering reveals distinct regime phenotypes.

Volatility is a reliable proxy for market stress
Classification generalizes across markets and time periods
failure_modes: Normal/abnormal boundary is continuous, not discrete
Regimes may shift meaning depending on asset class, time period, or market microstructure

claim: Analysis across 10 financial markets shows that Regime 1 (lower volatility) and Regime 2 (higher volatility) exhibit consistent statistical phenotypes (indicator ranges, distributions) when parameters like DC threshold θ are held constant.

title: Real-time regime tracking for market monitoring
claim: Directional Change indicators combined with a Naive Bayes classifier enable real-time, tick-by-tick regime tracking; probability thresholds (e.g., B-Simple, B-Strict variants) allow tunable sensitivity for early-warning signals.
support: Authors implement two variants of Naive Bayes classifier; test on DJIA, FTSE 100, S&P 500; successfully track regime transitions in real time.
mechanism: For each DC trend, compute probability of being in each regime via Naive Bayes; threshold probability to generate regime label; variants B-Simple and B-Strict trade off false positives vs. false negatives.
assumptions: Naive Bayes independence assumption holds for regime features
Historical frequency statistics are predictive of future regime membership
Probability thresholds can be tuned to desired sensitivity
failure_modes: Independence assumption violated if regime features are correlated
Past regime statistics may not predict future (non-stationary)
Lag between indicator and actual regime change not quantified
High false-positive rate may trigger spurious trading signals
validation: Tested on equity indices; regime transitions tracked successfully; but latency and false-positive rate for live systems not thoroughly analyzed.

title: Regime tracking lag and classification variants
claim: When regime transitions are tracked via Naive Bayes probability thresholds, there is inherent lag between regime onset and detection; B-Simple (immediate classification) and B-Strict (conservative thresholds) variants exhibit different lag-accuracy trade-offs.
support: Empirical testing on DJIA, FTSE 100, S&P 500 shows B-Simple has faster detection but higher false-positives; B-Strict is more conservative.
mechanism: B-Simple uses looser probability thresholds for immediate classification; B-Strict requires higher confidence; both inherit lag from Naive Bayes inference on accumulated DC trends.
assumptions: Lag is tolerable for intended trading system (minutes to hours)
Threshold tuning can be automated or learned from historical data
failure_modes: B-Simple may trigger too many false regime alarms
Lag may expand during low-volume periods or regime transitions
No principled way to select threshold without labeled regime data
validation: Comparative backtest results shown for indices; but optimal threshold not determined; post-implementation tuning recommended.

title: Regime change signals can reduce drawdown in algorithmic trading

mechanism: Regime-aware algorithms enter/exit positions on regime transitions; when regime shifts to abnormal (high volatility), algorithm may reduce exposure or tighten stops; this lowers peak losses.
assumptions: Regime transitions are predictive of future price movements or volatility
Entry/exit rules based on regime changes are optimal or near-optimal
Backtest assumptions (no slippage, instant fills, fixed transaction costs) hold in live trading
Money management (fixed lot size) is appropriate

support: The text presents several technical indicators and key macro variables, then describes both technical and fundamental analysis as critical to understanding market conditions.

title: Organization and journaling support better trading decisions
claim: An organized trader should prepare before entering a trade, keep a trading plan, and maintain a journal or record of trades to create feedback for later evaluation.
support: The psychology chapter explicitly recommends organization, pre-trade thinking, and maintaining a record of trades.

title: Realistic expectations require disposable capital and emotional distance
claim: The book argues that traders should use only disposable capital, avoid trades that cause sleeplessness, and treat each trade independently instead of becoming emotionally attached to outcomes.
support: Chapter 5 connects emotional control, realistic expectations, and disposable capital to healthier trading behavior.

title: Range trading should buy support and sell resistance in sideways markets
claim: Range trading is presented as buying near support and selling near resistance when the market lacks directional trend, while positions should be exited when the range breaks.
support: The strategy section defines the range, entry timing with oscillators, and risk management by exiting if support or resistance breaks.

title: Inside-bar continuation works best on daily charts with the trend
claim: The beginner inside-bar setup is described as most effective when traded on daily charts, after consolidation, and in the direction of the prevailing trend with a favorable risk-reward profile.
support: The book explicitly says to avoid sub-daily timeframes, focus on breakout after consolidation, and trade inside bars with the trend.

title: Pin bars need trend, structure, and value context
claim: Pin bars should not be traded blindly; the book recommends using them with the trend, after structure breaks, and from areas of value because not all pin bars carry the same information.
support: The text lists specific filters to improve pin-bar odds and warns against assuming every pin bar means reversal.

title: Breakouts should wait for confirmation and predefined exits
claim: Breakout trades should use confirmation such as retests or higher volume and should define profit-taking and stop-loss exits in advance to limit false-breakout losses.
support: The breakout section discusses false breakouts, confirmation, retests, volatility, and exit planning.

title: A usable trading signal needs complete trade instructions
claim: Forex trading signals are only actionable when they specify the currency pair, timing, direction, entry price, stop-loss, and target-profit level in a clear format.
support: The chapter defines signal payload fields and later says the best signals are simple, organized, and easy to follow.

title: Automated signal services save time but can fail opaquely
claim: Automated forex signals and robots can save time and support back-testing, but they are inflexible around unusual events and can fail through crashes, technical errors, stale logic, or fraudulent performance claims.
support: The chapter praises automation for speed and back-testing, but also warns that automated accounts can break down, crash, or keep trading through bad conditions.

title: Synchronize higher- and lower-timeframe signals before entering
claim: When using multiple charts, traders should align lower-timeframe entries with higher-timeframe directional bias instead of acting on conflicting signals across timeframes.

source.section: Choosing the Right Entry and Exit Points

support: The book explicitly recommends waiting for daily timing confirmation when the weekly chart provides the core direction.

title: Stop-losses should sit beyond the market invalidation level
claim: Risk management is not just placing tight stops near entry; stop-loss orders should be placed beyond the price level that market analysis says should not trade if the setup is valid.

source.section: Placing Stop-Loss Orders at the Right Price Levels

support: The chapter warns that excessively tight stops can knock traders out before the market reverses in their favor.

title: Keep per-trade risk small and consistent
claim: The book recommends risking only a small fraction of capital on each trade, with 1% to 2% of available capital presented as a good starting point, and keeping that risk level consistent across wins and losses.
support: Chapter 8 says traders should invest small percentages per trade, gives a 1%-2% example, and warns against increasing size after a winning streak.

title: Expectancy is a practical way to test system reliability
claim: The book offers expectancy as a simple measurement for trading-system reliability by combining win rate, average win, and average loss to estimate long-run dollars earned per dollar risked.
support: The chapter works a 10-trade example and concludes that positive expectancy indicates a potentially profitable system over time.

title: Crypto chapter makes freshness-sensitive operational claims
claim: The cryptocurrency chapter claims low fees, constant access, fast transfers, and growing adoption, but it also acknowledges severe price volatility, limited understanding, and adoption friction, making the material highly freshness-sensitive.
support: The chapter mixes promotional claims about control and low fees with explicit warnings about volatility, trust, and limited acceptance.

title: Trading without knowledge or a plan is a primary beginner failure mode
claim: The book treats uninformed trading and planless trading as foundational beginner mistakes and recommends education, demo practice, written plans, and realistic goals before live deployment.

source.section: Trading Without Much Knowledge; Trading Without a Plan

support: The chapter says traders should treat trading like a business, learn first, test plans in demo accounts, and follow the plan once live.

title: Overleverage, poor money management, and overtrading destroy accounts
claim: Beginners commonly blow up by risking too much per trade, trading borrowed or needed money, overtrading unfavorable markets, and ignoring risk-reward structure.

source.section: Lack of Money Management and Overtrading

support: The chapter explicitly criticizes overleverage, oversized single-trade risk, insufficient capitalization, and trading outside favorable plan conditions.

title: Choosing the wrong broker can strand capital or degrade execution
claim: A poor broker introduces scam risk, weak regulation, bad withdrawal access, unsuitable lot sizing, poor support, and possible dealing-desk conflicts, so traders should background-check and test brokers before depositing full capital.
support: The chapter recommends checking regulation, reviews, micro-lot support, dealing-desk behavior, and demo quality before trusting a broker.

title: Passive-income promises from forex are weakly supported
claim: The final chapter markets forex signals, robots, and social trading as routes to passive income, but the text provides little evidence for durable profitability and repeatedly admits that provider research and ongoing supervision are still necessary.

source.section: How to Make Money with Forex Trading to Create Passive Income

support: The chapter uses promotional language about passive income while simultaneously warning that not all providers or robots work as claimed.

title: Signals, robots, and social trading need provenance and oversight
claim: Even when traders outsource decisions to signals, robots, or social-copy trading, they still need to verify provider quality, monitor runtime behavior, and understand that automation and copied trades can fail or be fraudulent.

source.section: Forex Signals, Forex Robots, Social Trading

support: The chapter recommends researching providers and monitoring robots while warning that many robots are frauds and trusted traders are hard to identify.

title: ML as strategic capability in investment industry
claim: ML has become critical competitive advantage in investment; digital data explosion drives adoption across idea generation, alpha design, asset allocation, position sizing, strategy evaluation
support: Field evolved from narrow trade execution automation to comprehensive algorithmic strategies
mechanism: ML enables processing of broader data sources than classical methods
validation: Compare ML-managed AUM vs discretionary

title: Tick data regularization prevents look-ahead bias
claim: Raw tick data must be regularized into uniform bars (time, volume, dollar) to avoid look-ahead bias from irregular event timing
support: ITCH order book data requires time-normalization to reflect real decision points
mechanism: Non-uniform tick intervals create phantom information leakage; regularization aligns features to decision frequency
validation: Walk-forward IC stability across bar sizes

title: Four-category factor framework for alpha engineering
claim: Alpha factors categorize into: (1) momentum/sentiment, (2) value, (3) volatility/size, (4) quality. Each has domain-specific metrics and economic rationale
support: Systematic framework linking factors to market inefficiencies and tradeable premia
mechanism: Each factor exploits distinct market behavior: momentum=underreaction, value=fundamental mispricing, volatility=leverage effects, quality=risk-adjusted returns
validation: Cross-validate across universes (US/intl, caps, sectors); test comovement

title: Three classes of backtest failure: data, implementation, overfitting
claim: Backtests fail via: (1) data biases (look-ahead, survivorship, outliers, unrepresentative periods), (2) implementation issues (mark-to-market timing, trading costs), (3) data-snooping and overfitting

source.section: How to avoid the pitfalls of backtesting

support: Taxonomy of failure modes linked to specific remedies (purging, embargoing, cost models, deflated SR)
mechanism: Look-ahead: using future data at decision time. Survivorship: excluding failed assets. Overfitting: parameter selection inflates expected OOS performance
validation: Walk-forward; in/out IC; Deflated SR analysis

title: Deflated Sharpe Ratio for backtest performance estimation
claim: Use deflated Sharpe Ratio to adjust reported SR for multiple hypothesis testing bias and estimate true out-of-sample performance likelihood
support: Bailey et al. framework addresses the multiple testing problem in quantitative research; provides statistical correction for backtest selection bias
mechanism: Deflated SR = in-sample SR * sqrt((1 - phi) / (N - 1)) where N=number of trials, phi=autocorrelation; lower values indicate higher overfitting risk
assumptions: SR estimation error follows predictable distribution
Trial count is known or estimated
failure_modes: Does not account for cross-strategy correlation
validation: Retrospective: compare deflated SR predictions to realized 2-3 year OOS returns

title: Time series cross-validation with purging and embargoing for trading models
claim: Standard K-fold CV causes look-ahead bias in time series; use purging (exclude training obs overlapping test), embargoing (exclude obs adjacent to test window), and combinatorial CV
support: de Prado framework explicitly addresses temporal leakage in ML backtests; implemented in MLearning library
mechanism: Standard CV leaks information through overlapping train/test periods; purging removes contamination, embargoing creates buffer for decision lag
assumptions: Sufficient data for buffering after purging
Test set is representative after filtering
validation: Walk-forward: measure IC/Sharpe drop when CV is vs isn't applied

title: Linear regression for returns forecasting: regularization and multicollinearity
claim: OLS linear regression for returns requires L1/L2 regularization (Lasso/Ridge) to handle multicollinearity in factors; unregularized OLS amplifies noise in correlated predictors
support: Regularized regression balances fit and generalization; Lasso feature selection, Ridge shrinkage
mechanism: Correlated features inflate coefficient standard errors and out-of-sample variance; L1 shrinkage to zero, L2 toward zero
assumptions: Linear relationship between factors and returns
Regularization hyperparameter tunable on validation set
validation: Walk-forward validation with expanding window

title: ARIMA/GARCH for volatility and autoregressive returns forecasting
claim: ARIMA models autoregressive returns patterns; GARCH models volatility clustering and mean-reversion; both require stationarity testing and lag-order selection
support: ARIMA captures short-term mean-reversion, GARCH captures volatility regimes and leverage effects
mechanism: Autocorrelated returns (AR) and errors (MA); variance depends on past shocks and variance (GARCH); useful for intraday/options strategies
assumptions: Series is stationary or can be differenced
Lag order can be identified via AIC/BIC
validation: Backtest volatility-adjusted position sizing using GARCH conditional vol

title: Bayesian methods for uncertainty quantification in trading models
claim: Bayesian inference provides posterior distributions over model parameters and predictions; useful for decision-making under uncertainty and adaptive strategy adjustment
support: Posterior distributions quantify belief updates from data; credible intervals replace frequentist confidence intervals for directional bets
mechanism: Prior belief + likelihood from data -> posterior; predictive distribution integrates over parameter uncertainty
validation: Backtest risk-adjusted positions using posterior credible intervals

title: Decision trees and random forests for factor importance and non-linear returns
claim: Decision trees capture non-linear relationships and interactions; random forests reduce overfitting via ensembling; feature importance from permutation/Gini measures factor relevance

source.section: Tree-based models: decision trees and ensembles

support: RF handles high-dimensional factor spaces and interactions automatically; importance scores guide factor selection
mechanism: Trees partition feature space; multiple uncorrelated trees average predictions and reduce variance; Gini split importance ranks factors
failure_modes: Importance may reflect collinearity not causation
validation: Backtest portfolio using top-K features by importance

title: Gradient Boosted Machines (GBM) for trading: sequential error correction and hyperparameter sensitivity
claim: GBM improves on weak learners via sequential error minimization; sensitive to learning rate, tree depth, and sample fraction; requires careful tuning and validation
support: GBM state-of-art for supervised learning; but prone to overfitting if hyperparameters not tuned properly
mechanism: Each tree fits residuals from prior trees; shrinkage and subsampling regularize; sequential updates can amplify overfitting in financial data
failure_modes: Learning rate too high->instability, too low->slow
validation: Walk-forward tuning; compare GBM to RF baseline

title: Unsupervised learning for portfolio construction: PCA, clustering, and cointegration
claim: PCA reduces dimensionality and identifies uncorrelated principal component portfolios; K-means clustering groups similar securities; cointegration identifies pairs for mean-reversion
support: Unsupervised methods uncover structure without labels; useful for risk factor discovery and asset grouping
mechanism: PCA: linear combinations of correlated factors. Clustering: segment assets by features. Cointegration: long-run equilibrium + mean-reversion trading
validation: Backtest cointegration pairs; measure P&L and Calmar ratio

title: Information Coefficient (IC) and Rank IC for factor alpha measurement
claim: IC = correlation(factor, next return); Rank IC = rank correlation; high IC (>0.05) indicates alpha, measured in-sample and out-of-sample for validation
support: IC is industry standard for factor evaluation; avoids backtest biases by measuring direct signal-return correlation
mechanism: IC measures predictive power independent of portfolio construction and costs; normalized by factor and return distributions
assumptions: IC is stable across time periods
IC translates to portfolio returns (depends on portfolio weight distribution)
failure_modes: IC estimates noisy with few observations
validation: Cross-validate IC across time windows; compare IC to backtest Sharpe

title: Market data quality: OHLCV aggregation, survivorship bias, and corporate actions
claim: Price data must account for splits, dividends, and delistings; survivorship bias (only successful companies in current data) biases backtest returns upward
support: Comprehensive data cleaning essential for valid backtests; poor-quality data inflates reported performance
mechanism: Splits adjust prices downward; dividends adjust prices and returns; delistings remove failed stocks from dataset; combined effect: reported returns are optimistic
validation: Verify adjustment factors against corporate action records

title: Alternative data evaluation: coverage, latency, cost, and predictive power
claim: Non-traditional data (satellite, credit card, web) may signal future returns; validate with IC measurement, cost analysis, and regime tests before integration
support: Alternative data offers informational edges but requires careful vetting; high cost may offset alpha
mechanism: Coverage: what % of universe, latency: delay vs real-time, cost: subscription + data processing, alpha: IC and Sharpe contribution
assumptions: IC from alt data is repeatable
Data is available over backtest window
failure_modes: Look-ahead bias in alt data timestamps
validation: Walk-forward: measure IC decay as more managers use data

title: Transaction costs, slippage, and impact in backtest modeling
claim: Realistic cost modeling (commissions, spreads, market impact) essential; omitting costs overestimates Sharpe by 0.5-2x; impact models scale with position size and liquidity
support: Most backtest failures trace to cost underestimation; live performance trails backtest sharply when costs neglected
mechanism: Commissions: fixed/percentage per trade. Spread: bid-ask cost. Impact: price moves proportional to position; scales nonlinearly with size
assumptions: Cost functions are linear or monotonic
Fills occur at midpoint or better
validation: Compare backtest-to-live PnL drop; audit cost assumptions

title: Bias-variance tradeoff and regularization in ML-based trading models
claim: Underfitting (high bias) misses alpha; overfitting (high variance) captures noise. Regularization, early stopping, and validation set selection balance tradeoff.
support: Fundamental ML principle; critical in finance where noise dominates in returns
mechanism: Bias from simplified model; variance from fitting to training noise. Regularization shrinks toward simpler model; validation prevents overfitting
validation: Compare in-sample to out-of-sample performance metrics

title: Multi-factor linear regression and collinearity diagnosis
claim: In multi-factor models, high VIF (variance inflation factor, >5) indicates collinearity; use correlation matrix and eigenvalue analysis to identify and remove redundant factors
support: Practical diagnostic for factor selection; prevents unstable coefficient estimates and poor OOS generalization
mechanism: VIF = 1 / (1 - R^2) for each factor regressed on others; high VIF means factor is linear combination of others
assumptions: Removing correlated factors doesn't lose alpha
validation: Walk-forward: track correlation matrix stability and factor weights

title: NLP and sentiment analysis for trading: text preprocessing, feature extraction, and model selection
claim: Extract sentiment from news, social media, earnings calls; preprocess (tokenization, stopwords, stemming), vectorize (TF-IDF, embeddings), and model with SVM, Naive Bayes, or RNNs
support: Text sentiment correlates with short-term price movements; integration with quantitative signals improves Sharpe
mechanism: Sentiment scores from text models fed to portfolio allocation or rank-weighting; lagged sentiment captures market psychology
assumptions: Sentiment is predictive of next return
Model generalizes across periods and topics
failure_modes: Model overfitting to historical sentiment-return correlation
validation: Walk-forward validation; check for crowding effect (IC decay)

title: Topic modeling and latent semantic analysis for thematic portfolio construction
claim: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) extract topics from documents; topics can signal sector trends and correlated risk factors
support: Unsupervised discovery of document structure; enables thematic portfolio tilting and risk factor identification
mechanism: LDA: generative model with document-topic and topic-word distributions. NMF: factorization into non-negative components
assumptions: Optimal number of topics is identifiable
validation: Cross-validate topic stability; check out-of-sample coherence

title: Word embeddings and semantic similarity for feature engineering
claim: Word2Vec, GloVe, and contextual embeddings (BERT) encode semantic meaning; embeddings capture industry relationships, thematic coherence, and text-based alpha signals

source.section: Word embeddings and neural networks for NLP

support: Embeddings preserve linguistic relationships; enable vector-based portfolio similarity, sector clustering, and similarity-based trading signals
mechanism: Embeddings trained on large text corpora; semantic similarity via cosine distance; enables transfer learning to new text domains
assumptions: Semantic relationships correlate with tradeable patterns
failure_modes: Domain shift (embeddings trained on general text, applied to finance)
Crowding effect from widespread embedding use
validation: Out-of-sample test: compare embedding-based signals to baseline

title: Hyperparameter tuning: grid search, randomized search, and Bayesian optimization
claim: Systematic hyperparameter search essential; grid search exhaustive but slow, random search efficient, Bayesian optimization balances exploration/exploitation
support: Hyperparameter selection strongly affects model performance; careless tuning leads to severe overfitting
mechanism: Grid: evaluate all combinations in grid. Random: sample uniformly. Bayesian: model performance surface, sample high-promise regions
assumptions: Tuning effort is justified by performance gain
validation: Cross-validate hyperparameters; measure sensitivity to tuning set

title: Alphalens factor tearsheet for systematic factor evaluation
claim: Use Alphalens to compute IC, Sharpe, returns attribution by quantile and day-lag; identify factor decay and crowding effects
support: Alphalens open-source; enables reproducible factor validation without backtest artifacts
mechanism: Ranks factors, computes returns in forward windows, aggregates by quantile and lag, produces comprehensive diagnostics
validation: Cross-validate IC across time splits

title: Hierarchical clustering and dendrogram-based portfolio construction
claim: Hierarchical clustering groups correlated assets; dendrogram linkage methods (single, complete, average) affect grouping; enables minimum-variance portfolio at cluster level
support: Hierarchical clustering provides interpretable asset grouping; can improve risk-adjusted returns
mechanism: Agglomerative clustering: merge most similar pairs recursively; dendrogram visualizes hierarchy; cut at desired granularity
validation: Walk-forward clustering; measure realized correlation structure

title: Feature importance from tree ensembles: Gini vs. permutation importance
claim: Gini importance (split reduction) biased toward high-cardinality features; permutation importance (OOB prediction drop) is model-agnostic and more reliable for trading factors
support: Permutation importance avoids Gini bias; enables fair comparison across factor types (continuous, categorical)
mechanism: Gini: split information gain in tree. Permutation: shuffle feature, measure OOB error increase
failure_modes: OOB error not reliable with small datasets
validation: Measure IC of top factors by each importance metric

title: Walk-forward analysis and forward-looking bias in backtest optimization
claim: Standard backtest with parameter optimization on full history is forward-looking; walk-forward (expanding train, test on next period) prevents look-ahead bias in hyperparameter selection
support: Walk-forward is only defensible method for parameter optimization; otherwise backtest is invalid
mechanism: Expanding train window 1..T, validate T+1..T+K; retune parameters on each window
assumptions: Parameters optimized on future data are invalid
validation: Audit backtest code: confirm walk-forward structure

title: Stationarity testing and differencing for time series models
claim: Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test identifies unit root (non-stationarity); differencing (first/seasonal) removes trend; stationarity required for ARIMA and many models

source.section: Time series preprocessing: stationarity and differencing

support: Stationarity assumption critical for model validity; violation leads to spurious regression
mechanism: ADF tests H0: unit root present. P-value < 0.05: reject null, series is stationary. Differencing: X(t) = Y(t) - Y(t-1)
assumptions: Differenced series is suitable for modeling
failure_modes: ADF p-value unreliable with short series
validation: Train ARIMA on differenced series; check residuals for remaining autocorrelation

title: XGBoost and LightGBM: efficient gradient boosting for large-scale factor modeling
claim: XGBoost and LightGBM are production-grade GBM implementations with GPU support and built-in regularization; outperform hand-coded GBM on speed and generalization
support: Industrial standard; implemented in major trading platforms and research workflows
mechanism: XGBoost: L-BFGS optimizer, column subsampling. LightGBM: leaf-wise growth, GPU acceleration
assumptions: Data fits in memory or distributed storage
validation: Compare OOS Sharpe and training time

title: Factor crowding and mean reversion of alpha as strategy popularity increases
claim: Factors exhibit alpha decay over time; crowding (many managers implement same factor) compresses returns and increases correlation; diversification across factors mitigates
support: Empirical finding: published factor premiums decay after research visibility; alpha is finite and consumable
mechanism: Crowding: increased AUM chasing same signal, increased slippage and market impact, reduced alpha per unit capital
failure_modes: Crowding effect varies by factor type
validation: Backtest: simulate increasing AUM impact

title: Bid-ask spread, volume, and liquidity regime effects on trading signals
claim: Liquid assets (low spread, high volume) enable low-cost execution; illiquid regimes increase slippage; signal IC varies by liquidity; liquid subset may outperform due to lower costs
support: Liquidity is primary execution constraint; trading cost model essential for live performance
mechanism: Spread cost: (ask - bid) / mid. Slippage: (execution - mid) / mid. Both scale nonlinearly with order size
assumptions: Cost is proportional to liquidity metric
validation: Compare backtest to live execution cost

title: Copula models and tail dependence for portfolio construction
claim: Copulas model joint distributions of asset returns; tail dependence captures co-crash risk; useful for extreme risk management and drawdown minimization
support: Captures non-linear dependence missed by correlation; critical for tail risk
mechanism: Copula: joint distribution independent of marginals; enables separate modeling of extremes and normal regime
validation: Backtest during market crises; measure maximum drawdown

title: Machine learning pipeline for quantitative trading: data -> features -> model -> backtest -> deployment
claim: Structured workflow prevents data leakage and ensures reproducibility; each stage must validate before proceeding to next
support: Systematic pipeline design reduces operational risk and enables scaling
mechanism: Data cleaning -> feature engineering (alignment, lag) -> model selection/tuning (CV) -> backtest (walk-forward) -> live deployment
validation: Compare backtest-to-live performance; verify pipeline determinism

title: Lookahead bias and temporal alignment in factor and alternative data integration
claim: Factor release dates must precede decision times; alternative data timestamps subject to backfill; use trade date + N day lag, not price date, for alignment
support: Temporal misalignment is subtle and pervasive source of backtest overfitting; critical for credibility
mechanism: Earnings announced after market close (day T); backtest must use day T+1 close or day T+2 open, not day T close
failure_modes: Backfill in alt data (values updated retroactively)
validation: Rerun backtest with enforced lag; measure performance delta

title: Logistic regression for classification and position sizing in directional strategies
claim: Logistic regression outputs probability of up/down move; useful for position sizing and stop-loss automation; calibration essential (predicted prob matches realized freq)
support: Probabilistic output enables confidence-weighted position sizing; more nuanced than binary signals
mechanism: Sigmoid: P(y=1) = 1/(1+exp(-z)); output in [0,1]; calibration: predicted prob = realized freq
failure_modes: Probability estimates unstable in new regimes
validation: Backtest with position sizing by predicted probability

title: Combinatorial purged K-fold for unbiased ML model selection in backtests
claim: Combinatorial purged cross-validation (CPV) extends time-series CV with multiple train/test combinatorial splits; reduces variance of CV estimate
support: CPV provides more stable CV scores than single split; reduces overconfidence in model selection
mechanism: Multiple combinatorial purged splits; aggregate CV scores across splits; reduces noise
assumptions: Data is sufficient for many splits
validation: Cross-validate stability across different CPV configurations

title: Sentiment model drift and domain shift in deployed NLP systems
claim: Sentiment models trained on historical text may not generalize to new topics, events, or linguistic style changes; monitor model performance and retrain when drift detected
support: Model drift is primary source of live performance degradation in NLP-based strategies
mechanism: Language evolves (new slang), topics shift (pandemic, war), style changes (formal vs. casual); model trained on past text misclassifies new text
validation: Backtest sentiment model trained on 1-3 year windows; compare accuracy

title: Cross-validation strategy selection and nested CV for honest performance estimation
claim: Inner CV tunes hyperparameters; outer CV estimates generalization error; nested CV is only unbiased method
support: Nested CV prevents data snooping in hyperparameter selection; expensive but necessary for credible estimates
mechanism: Outer loop: split into train/test. Inner loop (on train): tune hyperparameters via CV. Report outer loop test error
failure_modes: Overfitting still possible if inner CV underfits
validation: Backtest both; compare OOS Sharpe to nested CV estimate

title: Stacking and blending for ensemble returns prediction
claim: Stacking: train meta-learner on base model predictions; blending: holdout set to train meta-learner; both combine weak learners into stronger ensemble
support: Ensembling multiple models often outperforms single best model; meta-learner learns to weight predictions
mechanism: Base models: RF, GBM, linear reg. Meta-learner: logistic reg or ridge on base outputs. Avoids overfitting via validation holdout
failure_modes: Base model correlation reduces ensemble benefit
validation: Compare ensemble IC to individual base model IC

title: Dimensionality reduction via PCA and variance preservation trade-off
claim: PCA retains k principal components explaining desired variance (e.g., 95%); reduces collinearity and computational cost; but loses interpretability
support: PCA is standard unsupervised dimensionality reduction; balances noise reduction and information retention
mechanism: Eigenvector decomposition of covariance; ordered by eigenvalue (explained variance); select cumulative variance threshold
validation: Plot cumulative explained variance; select k at elbow

title: Zipline backtesting framework: event-driven simulation and reproducibility
claim: Zipline is open-source backtester with event-driven architecture; enables reproducible, modular strategy development; integrated with Alphalens for factor analysis
support: Zipline is de facto standard for open-source Python backtesting; widely adopted in academic and industry research
mechanism: Event-driven: loop through market events (OHLC bars); execute trading logic; track positions and P&L
failure_modes: Zipline version changes break existing code
validation: Compare Zipline backtest to manual calculation

title: Book teaches complete trading plan from entry to exit with specific price levels
claim: Unlike most trading books, this book teaches specific action sequences including exact buy/sell prices rather than vague guidance like 'buy around here'

title: Supply-Demand Equilibrium and Price Discovery
claim: Modern markets are driven by supply-demand equilibrium; price discovery is fundamental to market operations. Increased technology and market participant access makes price discovery more efficient than historically.

title: Order Matching Algorithms
claim: Exchanges facilitate price discovery through order matching; matching algorithms (FIFO vs pro-rata) determine execution outcomes. Different order types (market, limit, iceberg, stop) route through matching engines with different priorities.

title: Algorithmic Trading Speed Risk
claim: Automated trading systems inherit market risk and operational risk; execution speed advantages can amplify losses when volatility spikes or systems malfunction.

title: Technical Indicator Fundamentals
claim: Technical indicators (SMA, EMA, RSI, MACD, Bollinger Bands) extract trading signals from price/volume. Simple Moving Average (SMA) averages price over N periods. Exponential Moving Average (EMA) weights recent prices more heavily.

title: RSI and MACD Signal Lag
claim: RSI and MACD rely on historical price patterns; overbought/oversold signals can lag during trending markets. Bollinger Bands may generate false breakout signals when volatility regime changes abruptly.

title: ML Indicator Overfitting Risk
claim: Machine learning models trained on historical indicators risk overfitting to past regimes; forward testing and out-of-sample validation essential before deployment.

title: Supervised Learning Feature Engineering
claim: Supervised learning (classification, regression) predicts price movements from features (price, volume, indicators). Feature engineering critical; raw indicators may contain multicollinearity and redundancy.

title: Data Leakage in ML Backtesting
claim: Data leakage (using future information to train) invalidates backtests; proper temporal separation of train/validation/test sets required; walk-forward validation recommended.

title: Momentum Strategy Volatility Scaling
claim: Momentum strategies exploit price trends; buy assets with rising prices, sell with falling prices. Volatility adjustment improves risk-adjusted returns; scaling position size inversely with volatility stabilizes portfolio returns.

title: Mean-Reversion Pair Trading
claim: Mean-reversion strategies assume prices revert to historical average; identify overbought/oversold conditions. Pair trading exploits mean-reversion between correlated assets; requires mean-reversion regime detection.

title: Statistical Arbitrage Cointegration
claim: Statistical arbitrage exploits pricing inefficiencies between correlated securities. Cointegration testing identifies stationary price spreads; trading when spread deviates from historical mean.

title: Execution Algorithms TWAP VWAP
claim: Execution algorithms minimize transaction costs and market impact. TWAP (Time-Weighted Average Price) distributes order over time window. VWAP (Volume-Weighted Average Price) aligns execution with market volume profile.

title: Execution Slippage Cost Impact
claim: Execution slippage (actual fill price vs model price) can erode strategy profitability; simulated transaction costs in backtest must account for realistic market impact and latency effects.

title: Risk Quantification Sharpe Drawdown VaR
claim: Risk metrics: Sharpe Ratio (return per unit volatility), Maximum Drawdown (peak-to-trough decline), Value-at-Risk (VaR, worst-case loss percentile). Portfolio volatility computed from asset correlations; diversification reduces joint risk.

title: Real-Time Risk Controls Position Limits
claim: Live trading requires real-time risk limits: position limits (max notional, max contracts), drawdown stops, Greeks hedging (delta, gamma, theta for derivatives). Breach triggers automatic order cancellation or liquidation.

title: VaR Tail Risk Limitations
claim: VaR underestimates tail risk during market stress; fat-tailed distributions and regime changes exceed VaR thresholds. Stress testing and scenario analysis necessary complements to VaR.

title: Modular Trading System Architecture
claim: Modular trading system architecture: data ingestion (feeds, market data) → signal generation (strategy logic) → execution (order router) → settlement (risk reconciliation). Decoupling enables independent testing and deployment.

title: Order Management System Gateway

title: Primary financial markets are where new securities and assets are sold by borrowers and sellers to investors

title: Debt vs Equity as fundamental investment choices

mechanism: Debt instruments have scheduled cash flows; equity has residual claims and unlimited upside
assumptions: Equity holders benefit from business growth

mechanism: Returns drive cash flows; risks discount expected value; relative value determines entry/exit points
assumptions: Assets are valued based on risk-adjusted expected cash flows

title: Three analytical approaches to investment decisions: fundamental, technical, and quantitative analysis

support: Classification of investor research methodologies
mechanism: Each approach encodes different information signals and assumptions about market efficiency
assumptions: Price history contains information about future returns

title: Long and short positions: definition and return mechanics

support: Foundational definition of directional exposure mechanics
mechanism: Long position has unlimited upside, limited downside (loss of principal); short position has unlimited loss potential, limited upside (sale price minus cost)
validation: Standard market mechanics

title: Governments issue bills (<=1 year), notes (<=10 years), and bonds (>10 years) to finance budget deficits

support: Foundational framework for fixed income markets
mechanism: Government debt maturity structure reflects borrowing needs and interest rate risk distribution

title: Currency markets reflect returns on bank deposits and government security holdings

validation: Standard international finance concept

Credit markets price company risk correctly

mechanism: Equity has no maturity, residual claim, and voting rights
validation: Foundational corporate finance concept

title: Hard assets (gold, commodities, real estate) are tangible alternatives to financial securities

title: Futures and forwards are derivative contracts for future delivery or settlement
